summary: Defines how the Extensible Provisioning Protocol is used to provision and manage domain names in a shared registry. It specifies the commands and their meanings for domains. It obsoletes an earlier version and is an Internet Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5731 defines how EPP commands manage domain objects in a shared repository. It specifies the XML data for checking, creating, renewing, transferring, and updating a domain, as well as the information returned by those operations.

subtitle: The EPP XML commands and attributes used to create, inspect, renew, transfer, and update domain objects.

tldr.problem: The base Extensible Provisioning Protocol defines command structures but not the domain objects or the meaning of commands applied to them.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5731 defines XML elements for domain attributes, status values, name servers, authorization information, and EPP query and transform commands.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5731 is Internet Standard STD 69, obsoletes RFC 4931, and builds on the base EPP specification in RFC 5730.

today: RFC 5731 is an Internet Standard (STD 69) that obsoletes RFC 4931. It builds on RFC 5730.

sections.title: Domain Objects and Name Servers
sections.content:
RFC 5731 is the EPP version 1.0 mapping for Internet domain names. It uses XML and defines the syntax and meaning of EPP commands for provisioning and managing domain names. The base EPP command and response structures are defined in RFC 5730.

Domain objects are superordinate to subordinate host objects. For example, a domain such as example.com can have a subordinate host such as ns1.example.com. The mapping requires actions that would break this relationship to be explicitly disallowed. Name servers can be represented as existing host objects or as host attributes.
sections.plainLanguage: This mapping gives EPP commands a defined meaning for domain names. It also defines how a domain refers to name-server host objects or their attributes.

sections.title: Domain Attributes and Status Values
sections.content:
A domain object has a name, status values, and related information such as contacts, name servers, authorization information, and validity period. A domain must always have at least one status. Statuses beginning with client can be set or cleared by the sponsoring client; statuses beginning with server are controlled by the server; other statuses are server-managed.

Examples include clientHold, which means DNS delegation information MUST NOT be published, inactive, which means delegation information is not associated with the object, and pendingTransfer, which means a transfer action is pending. The ok status cannot be combined with another status.

A validity period uses years or months and has a minimum value of 1 and maximum of 99, though a server may set a lower maximum. Authorization information is assigned when a domain is created and is used in transfer operations.
sections.plainLanguage: A domain record includes status labels that describe restrictions or work in progress. Some labels are controlled by the sponsoring client, while others are controlled by the server.

sections.title: Querying Domain Information
sections.content:
The check command asks whether one or more domain names can be provisioned. Its response includes an availability value and may include a reason. The result is only a hint because provisioning depends on server policy.

The info command returns domain details, including its status, contacts, name servers, and dates. The response may depend on who is asking and whether valid authorization information is provided. The transfer query reports the state of the most recent transfer, who requested it, who should act, and the time by which an automatic response will occur if it remains pending.
sections.plainLanguage: Clients can ask whether a name is available, request details about a domain, or check a transfer's status. The registry may show different details depending on the client's identity and authorization.

sections.title: Creating, Renewing, Transferring, and Updating
sections.content:
The create command supplies a domain name and authorization information, with optional registration period, name servers, registrant, and contacts. Referenced host and contact objects must already be known to the server. The renew command includes the current expiry date so repeated requests do not cause unintended multiple renewals.

The transfer command manages a change of sponsorship and MUST implicitly transfer subordinate host objects with the domain. The update command adds, removes, or changes attributes such as name servers, contacts, statuses, registrant, and authorization information. Unauthorized transform requests MUST be rejected with result code 2201.

A server SHOULD NOT delete a domain while subordinate hosts remain associated with it. It SHOULD indicate this relationship problem with result code 2305.
sections.plainLanguage: Transform commands create a domain, extend its registration, change its sponsoring client, or edit its attributes. A domain transfer also includes its subordinate host objects.

sections.title: When a Requested Action Needs Review
sections.content:
A server may accept a transform request but wait for human or third-party review before completing it. In that case it MUST return result code 1001 and set a matching pending status on the domain object. When the action finishes, the server MUST remove the pending status and notify the involved clients.

The server can queue a service message for retrieval with the poll command. The message includes whether the request was approved, the original transaction identifiers, and the time the review finished.
sections.plainLanguage: A registry can acknowledge a request before it completes. It marks the domain as pending and later sends a message saying whether the action was approved.

sections.title: XML Syntax and Namespaces
sections.content:
The formal syntax is an XML Schema representation of the domain mapping, suitable for validating EPP XML instances. The domain namespace is urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:domain-1.0. XML is case-sensitive, so element and attribute case must match the forms shown in the specification.

The RFC requires date-time values to use Coordinated Universal Time and the extended form with uppercase T and Z. It recommends UTF-8 when parser encoding support may be incompatible. Domain and host names must follow the naming requirements referenced by the document.
sections.plainLanguage: EPP uses XML elements in a registered domain namespace. The exact capitalization and date-time format matter, and UTF-8 is recommended where encoding support differs.

sections.title: Protecting Authorization Information
sections.content:
Authorization information is required when creating a domain and is used as an additional authorization check for some queries and transfers. If it is disclosed, someone may be able to make an unauthorized transfer or obtain information without authorization.

Clients and servers MUST store and exchange authorization information using high-grade encryption mechanisms. The mapping adds no other security services beyond those in the base EPP specification and the protocol layers used by EPP.
sections.plainLanguage: Domain authorization information can help approve a transfer or access a domain's details. Keep it private by protecting it in storage and during exchange.

items.label: Normal
items.desc: No pending operations or prohibitions; not combined with another status.

items.label: No delegation
items.desc: Delegation information is not associated with the domain.

items.label: Hold
items.desc: DNS delegation information MUST NOT be published.

items.label: Create pending
items.desc: The create action has been processed but is not complete.
